name: Zoe Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. First, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 27, and I work at Kerr Brothers, a dairy and potato farm run by two brothers, Neil and Ross. We milk about 180 cows with four milking robots, and grow potatoes on rented ground. I've been there 18 months, and before that I was on a pig farm for a year. I live with Sam, who's an electrician, and we're engaged, though we haven't set a date.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The robots do the milking, so my day is fetching the cows that don't go in on their own, cleaning, checking the robot alarms on the phone, and feeding calves. In spring and autumn I'm on the potato side, planting and then grading on the harvester. I like the calves, and I like that the robots take the 4am milking off us. What wears me out is the alarms, because the robot rings your phone at night if a cow's got stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things always get hyped. I'd say the robots on our farm are useful but they still need us. I might post a picture of a cow refusing to go in the robot, because that's my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think fine, nothing changes for me. I've already seen what machines do on a farm, and it's less than people think. My job is safe enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, learn the calving and the herd health side from Neil. Sam and I would keep saving and probably set a wedding date for next summer. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the normal version of the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already work with robots. What did you see happen when they came in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before my time, but Ross says they thought they'd lose two milkers. They didn't, the milkers just did different things, more fetching, more health checks, more data. One lad left because he hated the phone alarms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI yourself now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I ask a chatbot what an alarm code means sometimes, or to help with the herd notes. Ross uses it more than me.

S0.say: She'd say she's not surprised, because these things always get hyped. The robots on her farm are useful, but they still need people.
S0.think: Privately she thinks nothing changes for her, because she's already seen what machines do on a farm. Her job feels safe enough.
S0.do: Keeps going and learns calving and herd health from one of the farm owners. Keeps saving with her fiancé and sets a wedding date for next summer.
S0.feel: Calm. It's the normal version of the future.
S0.quote: I might post a picture of a cow refusing to go in the robot, because that's my life.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe works on a farm that already uses milking robots, so she judges each scenario against what she's seen. She uses AI casually, for alarm codes and notes. Her plans are steady and practical: learn more, save, set a wedding date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the same as when the milking robots came in: some jobs change, people adjust. I'd say the farms that do it well keep their good staff. That's what I've seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I'm all right. Our farm already went through this, and the staff stayed. The potato side might change, but there'll still be cows that won't go in the robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever new tool the farm brought in, once Ross had tried it. I'd use the AI stuff a bit more for herd records. And we'd keep saving and still get married next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit curious about what changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job do you think changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The potato grading, probably. There's already cameras that sort potatoes by size and damage. That's me on the harvester in October, picking out stones and rotten ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Kerr Brothers you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Davey, who does most of the potato work. He's 50 and it's what he's done his whole life. He'd hate learning a screen, and I'd hate to see him go.

S1.say: She'd say it's the same as when the milking robots came in: some jobs change and people adjust. Farms that do it well keep their good staff.
S1.think: Privately she thinks she's all right, because her farm already went through this and kept its staff. The potato side might change, but cows will still need fetching.
S1.do: Learns whatever new tool the farm brings in once an owner has tried it, and uses AI more for herd records. Keeps saving and goes ahead with the wedding next summer.
S1.feel: Fine, with some curiosity about what changes.
S1.quote: There'll still be cows that won't go in the robot.
S1.fieldNote: Her calm here is earned from experience, not wishful thinking. She pinpoints potato grading as the next task to go, and her own October work with it. Her worry for Davey shows she sees who pays the cost even when she doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is different from the milking robots, it's everything at once. I'd say people need help to get through it, but I wouldn't be on a soapbox. Mostly I'd talk to Sam and my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means the bits of my job the robots couldn't do, they can now. Fetching cows, feeding calves, all of it. I'd be out of work within a year, probably, and so would half the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every penny and hold on to the cushion we've got. I'd ask Sam about going in with him, training as an electrician's mate, because someone has to wire all these robots in, at least for a while. I'd stay at Kerr's as long as they wanted me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, we've got money, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sam's an electrician. Does that matter here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's my way out. He's always said I'm good with wiring on the fences. For two or three years there'll be more robots needing installing than people to install them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd do it small, at the registry office, and keep the money. My mum would be upset about the dress. But two years is no time to spend on a party.

S2.say: She'd say this is different from the milking robots, because it's everything at once. People need help, but she wouldn't be on a soapbox about it.
S2.think: Privately she thinks the bits of her job robots couldn't do, they now can. She expects to be out of work within a year, along with half the farm.
S2.do: Saves every penny and holds on to her cushion. Trains as an electrician's mate with her fiancé to install robots, and has a small registry-office wedding instead of a big one.
S2.feel: Anxious, but not falling apart, because they have money.
S2.quote: For two or three years there'll be more robots needing installing than people to install them.
S2.fieldNote: The fast version breaks her comparison with the milking robots, and she says so. Her escape route is practical and close to home: her partner's trade. She trims the wedding rather than cancelling it, which says a lot about her steadiness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. I'd tell younger ones at the farm to learn something technical alongside the animals. I'd say it in the tea room, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out of it all right. I'd have time to get a proper electrical qualification, not just be Sam's helper. That's a real change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for an evening electrical course at the college and use AI tools a bit more to learn the theory. I'd keep working at Kerr's and keep saving. We'd still have a proper wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between being Sam's mate and being an electrician. With two years I'd be carrying his toolbox. With five I'd have my own ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay on the farm or leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stay as long as I could, and then go. I'd want to be the one who services the farm robots in the area. That way I'm still on farms, just doing a different thing.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. She'd tell younger workers to learn something technical alongside the animals.
S3.think: Privately she thinks she'd come out of it all right, with time to get a proper electrical qualification. That's a real change from being a helper.
S3.do: Signs up for an evening electrical course in the first year and uses AI tools to learn the theory. Keeps working at the farm, keeps saving and still has a proper wedding.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but able to see a way through.
S3.quote: With two years I'd be carrying his toolbox. With five I'd have my own ticket.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns a stopgap into a qualification. She'd still like to stay on farms, just in a different role. The wedding comes back, which tracks how secure she feels in this version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's plan sensibly and not panic. I'd say the farms and the colleges should work together on training. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't worry me much. I'll be 37, I'll know the farm well, and I've got Sam and our savings. I'd change when the change was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Kerr's, get properly good at herd health, and use the AI tools as they get better. We'd buy a house in the next couple of years. I'd do the electrical course later, once I could see it was needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little voice saying don't get lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out, would you still do the electrical course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but not straight away. I'd wait till I saw robots doing the jobs they couldn't do before. Then I'd go, and I'd still have years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Herd manager somewhere, or servicing robots. Maybe with a kid or two. Probably still answering a phone at 3am because a cow's stuck.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty of time, so plan sensibly and don't panic. Farms and colleges should work together on training.
S4.think: Privately it doesn't worry her much, because she'll be experienced, has a partner and savings. She'd change when the change was real.
S4.do: Keeps going at the farm, gets good at herd health and uses AI tools as they improve. Buys a house in the next couple of years and saves the electrical course for later.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a small voice warning her not to get lazy.
S4.quote: Probably still answering a phone at 3am because a cow's stuck.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she goes back to her steady pattern of waiting for proof before acting. She's aware this could slide into complacency and says so. Buying a house is her main move, which fits her secure position.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to learn anything properly and the wedding goes small. What would help is cheap evening courses in practical trades, so people like me can switch without stopping work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we already know. Some of us have been working with robots for years. Nobody asks the people who fetch the cows that won't go in.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the people who fetch the cows that won't go in.
portrait: Zoe Walsh is a 27-year-old junior dairy and potato worker at Kerr Brothers, a farm that already milks with robots. She's engaged to Sam, an electrician, and they have solid savings. Pragmatic and steady, she judges every scenario against what she's seen of machines on her own farm, and she stays calm through the slower changes. The two-year AGI picture makes her anxious and pushes her towards training with Sam, while with more time she plans a proper electrical qualification and, eventually, a house.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to learn anything properly.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap evening courses in practical trades, so people can switch jobs without stopping work.
